claim: The time-dependent rate I(t) of origin firing per length of unreplicated DNA presents a universal bell shape in eukaryotes.
source: The time-dependent rate I(t) of origin firing per length of unreplicated DNA presents a universal bell shape in eukaryotes that has been interpreted as the result of a complex time-evolving interaction between origins and limiting firing factors.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the abstract and is supported by citation to Goldar et al., 2009 in the introduction.

claim: Normal diffusion of replication fork components towards localized potential replication origins can account for the I(t) universal bell shape.
source: Here, we show that a normal diffusion of replication fork components towards localized potential replication origins (p-oris) can more simply account for the I(t) universal bell shape, as a consequence of a competition between the origin firing time and the time needed to replicate DNA separating two neighboring p-oris.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by simulations and experimental data comparisons presented in the results.

claim: The I(t) maximal value is predicted to be the product of the replication fork speed with the squared p-ori density.
source: We predict the I(t) maximal value to be the product of the replication fork speed with the squared p-ori density.
evidence: This prediction is derived theoretically in Equation 5 and tested against simulations and experimental data.

claim: The relation I_max = v*ρ_0^2 is robustly observed in simulations and experimental data for several eukaryotes.
source: We show that this relation is robustly observed in simulations and in experimental data for several eukaryotes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2c and Table 1, showing agreement across multiple species.

claim: Fork-component recycling and potential origins localization are sufficient spatial ingredients to explain the universality of DNA replication kinetics.
source: Our work underlines that fork-component recycling and potential origins localization are sufficient spatial ingredients to explain the universality of DNA replication kinetics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the work, supported by the modeling results and comparisons with experimental data.

claim: Eukaryotic DNA replication is a stochastic process.
source: Eukaryotic DNA replication is a stochastic process (Hyrien et al., 2013; Hawkins et al., 2013; Hyrien, 2016b).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Prior to entering S-phase, a number of DNA loci called potential origins are licensed for DNA replication initiation.
source: Prior to entering the S(ynthesis)-phase of the cell cycle, a number of DNA loci called potential origins (p-oris) are licensed for DNA replication initiation (Machida et al., 2005; Hyrien et al., 2013; Hawkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: During S-phase, pairs of replication forks performing bi-directional DNA synthesis start from a subset of the p-oris in response to origin firing factors.
source: During S-phase, in response to the presence of origin firing factors, pairs of replication forks performing bi-directional DNA synthesis will start from a subset of the p-oris, the active replication origins for that cell cycle (Machida et al., 2005; Hyrien et al., 2013; Hawkins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Origin passivation forbids origin firing in already replicated regions.
source: Note that the inactivation of p-oris by the passing of a replication fork called origin passivation, forbids origin firing in already replicated regions (de Moura et al., 2010; Hyrien and Goldar, 2010; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: A bimolecular reaction between a diffusing firing factor and a p-ori results in an origin firing event in the model.
source: In our modeling of replication kinetics, a bimolecular reaction between a diffusing firing factor and a p-ori results in an origin firing event; then each half of the diffusing element is trapped and travels with a replication fork until two converging forks merge (termination, Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: A molecular mechanism explaining the synchronous recruitment of firing factors to both replication forks was recently proposed, supporting the bimolecular scenario for p-ori activation.
source: A molecular mechanism explaining the synchronous recruitment of firing factors to both replication forks was recently proposed (Araki, 2016), supporting the bimolecular scenario for p-ori activation.
evidence: This cites recent work supporting the modeling assumptions.

claim: The requirement for a larger number of origins can be met by some level of random initiation or initiation events away from mapped origins due to helicase mobility.
source: Apart from the unexpected activity of Dubious origins, the requirement for a larger number of origins can be met by some level of random initiation (Czajkowsky et al., 2008) or initiation events away from mapped origins due to helicase mobility (Gros et al., 2015; Hyrien, 2016a).
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations, supported by citations.

claim: Even though 829 p-oris are needed in S. cerevisiae, on average only 352 origins have fired by the end of S-phase.
source: It is to be noted that even if 829 p-oris are needed, on average only 352 origins have fired by the end of S-phase.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations.

claim: Experimental data points' deviation from Equation (5) is smaller than the deviation due to specific p-oris distributions.
source: We can observe that experimental data points' deviation from Equation (5) is smaller than the deviation due to specific p-oris distributions.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2c comparing experimental data with simulations using different distributions.

claim: The model assumes all p-oris are governed by the same rule of initiation resulting from physicochemically realistic particulars of their interaction with limiting replication firing factors.
source: Our model assumes that all p-oris are governed by the same rule of initiation resulting from physicochemically realistic particulars of their interaction with limiting replication firing factors.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the model.

claim: In yeast, replication kinetics along chromosomes were robustly reproduced in simulations where each replication origin fires following a stochastic law with parameters that change from origin to origin.
source: In yeast, replication kinetics along chromosomes were robustly reproduced in simulations where each replication origin fires following a stochastic law with parameters that change from origin to origin (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This cites previous modeling work.

claim: The heterogeneity between origins is captured by the Multiple-Initiator Model where origin firing time distribution is modeled by the number of MCM2-7 complexes bound at the origin.
source: Interestingly, this heterogeneity between origins is captured by the Multiple-Initiator Model where origin firing time distribution is modeled by the number of MCM2-7 complexes bound at the origin (Yang et al., 2010; Das et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites previous modeling work.

claim: The universal bell-shaped temporal rate of replication origin firing can be explained irrespective of species-specific spatial heterogeneity in origin strength.
source: Our results show that the universal bell-shaped temporal rate of replication origin firing can be explained irrespective of species-specific spatial heterogeneity in origin strength.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Current successful modeling of chromosome organization of DNA replication timing relies on heterogeneities in origins' strength and spatial distributions.
source: Note, however, that current successful modeling of the chromosome organization of DNA replication timing relies on heterogeneities in origins' strength and spatial distributions (Bechhoefer and Rhind, 2012).
evidence: This cites previous modeling approaches.

claim: 3D simulations with explicit diffusion of firing factors confirmed the physical relevance of the minimal modeling and the validity of its predictions for Xenopus embryo and S. cerevisiae.
source: As shown in Figure 2 (a,b) for Xenopus embryo and S. cerevisiae, results confirmed the physical relevance of our minimal modeling and the validity of its predictions when the 3D diffusion of the firing factors is explicitly taken into account.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a,b comparing 3D simulations with the well-mixed model.

claim: Modeling of replication timing profiles in human was successfully achieved in a model with both inhibition of origin firing 55 kb around active forks and an enhanced firing rate further away up to a few 100 kb.
source: Modeling of replication timing profiles in human was recently successfully achieved in a model with both inhibition of origin firing 55 kb around active forks, and an enhanced firing rate further away up to a few 100 kb (Löb et al., 2016) as well as in models that do not consider any inhibition nor enhanced firing rate due to fork progression (Gindin et al., 2014; Miotto et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites previous modeling work.

claim: In S. cerevisiae and S. pombe, a higher firing rate has been reported near origins that have just fired.
source: For example in S. cerevisiae (Knott et al., 2012) and in S. pombe (Kaykov and Nurse, 2015), a higher firing rate has been reported near origins that have just fired (but see Yang et al. (2010)).
evidence: This cites experimental observations.

claim: In mammals, megabase chromosomal regions of synchronous firing were first observed a long time ago.
source: In mammals, megabase chromosomal regions of synchronous firing were first observed a long time ago (Huberman and Riggs, 1968; Hyrien, 2016b) and the projection of the replication program on 3D models of chromosome architecture was shown to reproduce the observed S-phase dynamics of replication foci (Löb et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites historical and recent experimental observations.

claim: Profiling of replication fork directionality obtained by Okazaki fragment sequencing suggested that early firing origins located at the border of TADs trigger a cascade of secondary initiation events propagating through the TAD.
source: Recently, profiling of replication fork directionality obtained by Okazaki fragment sequencing have suggested that early firing origins located at the border of Topologically Associating Domains (TADs) trigger a cascade of secondary initiation events propagating through the TAD (Petryk et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites recent experimental observations.

claim: Early and late replicating domains were associated with nuclear compartments of open and closed chromatin.
source: Early and late replicating domains were associated with nuclear compartments of open and closed chromatin (Ryba et al., 2010; Boulos et al., 2015; Goldar et al., 2016; Hyrien, 2016b).
evidence: This cites experimental observations.

claim: In human, replication timing U-domains (0.1–3 Mb) were shown to correlate with chromosome structural domains and chromatin loops.
source: In human, replication timing U-domains (0.1–3 Mb) were shown to correlate with chromosome structural domains (Baker et al., 2012; Moindrot et al., 2012; Pope et al., 2014) and chromatin loops (Boulos et al., 2013, Boulos et al., 2014).
evidence: This cites experimental observations.

claim: For Xenopus embryo simulations, p-ori positions are randomly sampled so that each simulated S-phase corresponds to a different positioning of the p-oris.
source: For Xenopus embryo, the p-ori positions are randomly sampled, so that each simulated S-phase corresponds to a different positioning of the p-oris.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology.

claim: For S. cerevisiae simulations, the p-ori positions are identical for each simulation and are taken from the OriDB database.
source: For S. cerevisiae, the p-ori positions, identical for each simulation, are taken from the OriDB database (Siow et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology with citation to the data source.
